stem.text: Let In = ∫01 (1 + t)n sin πt dt, where n is a non-negative integer.

points.text: In = [–(1/π)(1+t)n cos πt]01 + (n/π) ∫01 (1+t)n–1 cos πt dt; applies integration by parts (limits may be missing); M1 for correct trigonometric functions and powers of (1+t)
In = (1/π)(2n + 1) + (n/π)[(1/π)(1+t)n–1 sin πt]01 – (n/π) ∫01 (1/π)(n–1)(1+t)n–2 sin πt dt; applies integration by parts again; M1 for correct trigonometric functions and powers of (1+t)
In = (1/π)(2n + 1) – (1/π2)n(n–1)In–2 ⇒ π2In = π(2n + 1) – n(n–1)In–2; AG, must have seen limits and correct use of brackets, CWO

explanation.text: This is a classic reduction-formula derivation: integrate by parts twice. The first integration by parts peels one power of (1+t) off using cos πt as the derivative of sin πt reversed; the second peels another power off, bringing back sin πt and reproducing a multiple of I_{n-2}.

reasoningChain: First integration by parts: let u = (1+t)^n, dv = sin πt dt, so du = n(1+t)^{n-1}dt, v = –(1/π)cos πt. Evaluate the boundary term and keep the remaining integral.
The boundary term at t=1 gives (–1/π)(2^n)(cos π) = (1/π)(2^n), and at t=0 gives (–1/π)(cos 0) = –1/π; combined this is (1/π)(2^n+1).
Second integration by parts on the remaining ∫(1+t)^{n-1}cos πt dt: let u = (1+t)^{n-1}, dv = cos πt dt, so v = (1/π)sin πt; the boundary term vanishes because sin 0 = sin π = 0.
What remains is –(n(n-1)/π²)∫(1+t)^{n-2}sin πt dt = –(n(n-1)/π²)I_{n-2}, which combines with the first boundary term to give the stated formula after multiplying through by π².

inferredMistakes.text: Losing a sign when integrating cos πt (its antiderivative is +sin πt/π, not –sin πt/π), which flips the sign of the whole reduction term.
Not writing the boundary terms explicitly with limits before evaluating, so the cos π = –1 substitution gets missed and the (2^n+1) term comes out wrong.

π2I2 = π(22 + 1) – 2(2–1)I0 [= 5π – 4/π]; uses reduction formula from (a)

Substitute n=2 into π²Iₙ = π(2ⁿ+1) – n(n–1)Iₙ₋₂ from part (a), using I₀ for I_{n-2}.
Solve for I₂ by dividing through by π².
